chunks: Capacitor differential equation. The question: What is the differential equation for a capacitor?
The defining equation of a capacitor is i equals C dv over dt . The current through it equals its capacitance times how fast the voltage across it is changing.
If the voltage is steady, no current flows. If the voltage changes quickly, a lot of current flows. This one equation explains most of what capacitors do.
Go back to the bucket from "What capacitance is". The water level is the voltage and the flow from the hose is the current.
The level rises only while water flows in, and a wide bucket (a large capacitance) needs more flow to raise its level at the same speed. Shut the hose and the level stays put.
The level can never jump instantly, because that would take an infinitely strong flow. A real capacitor leaks a little, like a bucket with a pinhole; the ideal one does not.
While +1 milliamps flows, v rises at 1 volts/ms; when the current flips to minus 1 milliamps, v falls at the same rate.
The capacitor integrates the current: flat segments of i become straight slopes of v. Here both traces are normalized to ±1 so the shapes line up; the triangle actually swings ±0.
Rate of change ( dv over dt ): how many volts per second the voltage is rising or falling. Capacitance (C): how much current you need per volt per second.
Time constant ( RC ): the natural time scale of a resistor charging a capacitor. Open circuit: no current flows. A charged capacitor at steady DC looks like this.
Continuity: a capacitor's voltage cannot jump instantly.
Push a constant 1 milliamps into a 1 microfarads capacitor. Then dv over dt equals i over C equals 0. 001 over 10 to the -6 equals 1000 volts/s, which is 1 volts per millisecond.
After 5 milliseconds the voltage is 5 volts. Stop the current and the voltage stays at 5 volts, because no current means no change. That is the whole idea.
"It's i equals C dv over dt : current through a capacitor is proportional to the rate of change of its voltage. You get it by differentiating Q equals CV .
The integral form is v equals v(0) plus 1 over C the integral of i dt , so the capacitor integrates current and remembers its initial voltage.
Consequences: constant voltage means zero current, so it's open at DC; constant current makes a linear ramp; and voltage can't jump instantly.
With a resistor it gives RC dv over dt plus v equals V s , the exponential RC response."
